body.statement: For every input in \(\mathfrak I_{\mathrm{rep}}\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), the construction \(\mathsf C_\varepsilon\) terminates. With explicitly chosen \(\zeta_{\mathrm{tail}},\zeta_{\mathrm{quad}},\zeta_{\mathrm{round}}>0\), every Gaussian rectangle call to \(\operatorname{GRect}\) returns an outward interval whose width is bounded by the sum of those three budgets, and the propagated certificate returns an interval containing \(V^*\) with width at most \(\varepsilon\), an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal feasible design and Gaussian rule, and an outer finite union of design cells containing every minimizer of \(L\). No termination claim is made for an opaque real input or an oracle-free compact set.
body.justification: The theorem places the numerical claim on an effective domain and makes every Gaussian probability and accumulated error auditable.
body.gap: Masten proposes computational-game methods and Kato certifies a particular three-arm comparison, but neither gives a general two-sided grid theorem for a design-indexed correlated policy game.
body.consumer: A trial designer can audit the claimed regret value, feasible rates, and all surviving optimal-design cells at a declared tolerance.
body.proof_tex:
Let an effectively represented instance be fixed. The floor \(r_{ax}\ge\rho\), eta positivity, distinct support values, and \(\operatorname{rank}(F)=d\) give computable constants
\[
0<\lambda_0:=\lambda_{\min}\{\Sigma(\mathbf1)\}
\le\lambda_{\min}\{\Sigma(r)\},\qquad
\lambda_{\max}\{\Sigma(r)\}\le
\Lambda_0:=\lambda_{\max}\{\Sigma(\rho\mathbf1)\}.
\]
Writing \(H_{ax}=p_x\sigma^2_{ax}(q^0)d_xd_x^\top/e_{ax}\), direct differentiation of \(1/r_{ax}\) gives
\[
\lVert\Sigma(r)-\Sigma(s)\rVert_F
\le C_r\lVert r-s\rVert_\infty,
\qquad C_r=\rho^{-2}\sum_{a,x}\lVert H_{ax}\rVert_F.
\]
If \(S,T\succeq\lambda_0I\) and \(\lVert T-S\rVert_F\le\lambda_0/2\), put \(E=S^{-1/2}(T-S)S^{-1/2}\). Since \(\lVert E\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le1/2\) and \(u-\log(1+u)\le u^2\) for \(|u|\le1/2\),
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\{N(h,T),N(h,S)\}
\le\frac12\lVert E\rVert_F^2.
\]
The elementary entropy-to-total-variation inequality proved in the Gaussian-characterization argument therefore yields
\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}\{N(h,T),N(h,S)\}
\le\frac{\lVert T-S\rVert_F}{2\lambda_0}.
\]
With \(U=\max_{h\in\mathcal H}\lVert h\rVert_\infty\) and \(R_0=2U\), the loss is bounded by \(R_0\) and is two-Lipschitz in \(h\). Equal-covariance Gaussian shifts similarly give the uniform state modulus
\[
|R(h,\delta)-R(g,\delta)|
\le K_H\lVert h-g\rVert_\infty,
\qquad K_H=2+\frac{R_0\sqrt d}{2\sqrt{\lambda_0}}.
\]

The projection \(P_B\) is the identity on \(\mathcal R_B\) and maps the full box onto it. If \(B=\rho\) it is constant. If \(B>\rho\), its two smooth pieces and matching boundary have the computable sup-norm Lipschitz bound \(1+(1-\rho)/(B-\rho)\). Thus a rational full-box mesh gives a finite certified covering mesh of \(\mathcal R_B\). The preceding covariance bound turns its covering radius \(\delta_r\) into design error
\[
E_{\mathrm{des}}=\frac{R_0C_r\delta_r}{2\lambda_0}.
\]

Choose \(T>U\). Every relevant Gaussian has
\[
P\{Z\notin[-T,T]^d\}\le2d\exp\left\{-\frac{(T-U)^2}{2\Lambda_0}\right\}=:p_T.
\]
Tile the cube exactly by rational cubes of side \(\gamma\). Coordinatewise averaging is an \(L^1\)-contraction, and the fundamental theorem of calculus gives
\[
\lVert f-\bar f\rVert_1
\le\gamma\sum_{j=1}^d\lVert\partial_jf\rVert_1
\le\frac{d\gamma}{\sqrt{\lambda_0}}.
\]
Consequently every measurable rule has a rectangle-constant approximation, with one fixed outside action, whose risk differs uniformly by at most
\[
E_{\mathrm{obs}}=R_0\left(p_T+\frac{d\gamma}{\sqrt{\lambda_0}}\right).
\]

At one design-grid point, let \(v(r)\) be the finite zero-sum game value using a \(\xi\)-net of \(\mathcal H\) and these observation rectangles. The two approximation directions are
\[
v(r)-E_{\mathrm{obs}}\le L(r)\le v(r)+K_H\xi.
\]
Indeed, averaging an arbitrary rule proves the left inequality, whereas evaluating the optimal rectangle rule at a nearest state-net point proves the right one. Each Gaussian rectangle probability is enclosed by \(\operatorname{GRect}\). Cholesky conditioning reduces the integral to a compact iterated integral after tails of total mass at most \(\zeta_{\mathrm{tail}}\) are removed. On that compact set all required Gaussian derivatives have explicit finite algebraic bounds; repeated subdivision therefore makes the quadrature width at most \(\zeta_{\mathrm{quad}}\), and increasing interval precision makes accumulated rounding width at most \(\zeta_{\mathrm{round}}\). Hence every call terminates with the asserted outward width.

The resulting finite linear program has rational interval coefficients. Rational primal and dual feasible vectors certify lower and upper values by weak duality; subdivision and increased precision reduce their gap to any prescribed \(E_{\mathrm{LP}}>0\). If the maximum rowwise probability-enclosure error is \(e_P\), its risk contribution is at most \(E_P=R_0e_P\). If \(v_{\mathrm{grid}}\) is the smallest certified finite-game value on the design grid, the proved global enclosure is
\[
v_{\mathrm{grid}}-E_{\mathrm{obs}}-E_{\mathrm{des}}-E_{\mathrm{LP}}-E_P
\le V^*\le
v_{\mathrm{grid}}+K_H\xi+E_{\mathrm{LP}}+E_P.
\]
Every term is effective and tends to zero under refinement. Enumerating refinements until their sum is at most \(\varepsilon\) therefore terminates and returns an interval of width at most \(\varepsilon\), together with the displayed feasible grid design and its certified rule.

Finally cover \(\mathcal R_B\) by the finitely many projected design cells. For each cell, subtract \(E_{\mathrm{des}}\) for its verified radius from its finite-game lower bound, and discard the cell only if this lower bound exceeds the global upper bound. A true minimizer can never be discarded, so the surviving finite union contains every minimizer. This is an objective certificate only; no distance-to-optimizer assertion has been used. Opaque reals or an unrepresented compact set do not permit the enumerations above, exactly as excluded in the claim.
